title: Compact tool ergonomics and structured response — PRD scratch
summary: A compact, developer-first PRD that defines an SDK and streaming surface for low-latency tool-calls with typed partial outputs and a hydration-driven client resume model.
body:
Context and motivation:

We’ve seen many host-side streaming and tool-calling designs converge on large, flexible protocols that are hard for client teams to adopt: heavy frames, complex rollback semantics, and unclear ergonomics for mobile/edge clients. This draft proposes a compact surface and SDK patterns focused on three developer priorities: predictable latency, simple tool-call choreography, and structured partial outputs that can be validated incrementally.

Problem statement:

- Mobile and low-bandwidth clients need a minimal handshake and small frame sizes to avoid jitter and retries.
- Tool-calling semantics are brittle in face of network interruptions: partial tool results should be usable immediately and resumable without expensive replays.
- SDK ergonomics are inconsistent: teams either implement their own fragile client-side reassembly logic or embed heavy runtimes.

Goals (what success looks like):

- Provide an API/SDK that reduces client integration time by 50% for tool-enabled streaming flows.
- Reduce token-level overhead on streaming transport by 30% through compact frames and delta encoding.
- Support resumable tool-call flows where partial tool output can be safely consumed and later reconciled.
- Telemetry-first: expose a small set of events that map directly to SLA and cost metrics (latency, tool wall-time, fallback rate).

Non-goals:

- This PRD does not redesign server-side scheduling or batching heuristics. It assumes the runtime will continue to perform batching and routing optimizations.
- Not trying to replace the full typed-frame protocol used by internal heavy-duty SDKs — this is a thin, stable surface for product integrations.

User personas and stories:

- Mobile app engineer (fast onboarding): "I want to add a quick 'smart reply' feature that calls a knowledge tool and streams partial suggestions to the UI without maintaining complex session state."
- Platform engineer (enterprise): "I need predictable fallbacks when a private tool is unreachable and clear telemetry to justify cost changes."

Product approach overview:

1) Compact frames: define two minimal frame kinds — CONTROL and PAYLOAD. CONTROL frames include lightweight handshake, commit tokens, and resume cursors. PAYLOAD frames carry typed fragments: narrative text, structured JSON snippets (schema refs), and tool capsules (opaque IDs + small metadata). Every PAYLOAD frame is delta-encoded relative to prior frames in the same session to reduce size.

2) Hydration-driven resume: clients receive compact hydration tokens (short opaque strings) at checkpoints. A hydration token encodes a server checkpoint pointer and minimal assertions (hashes of last-committed fragments). On resume, client presents the token; server returns a compact reconciliation delta (only frames since the checkpoint) or a canonical checkpoint if reconciliation fails.

3) Tool-call capsules and lease tokens: When a model requests a tool, the server emits a TOOL_CALL frame containing a tool_id, ephemeral lease_token (short ttl), and call_params summary. Tool backends respond with TOOL_RESULT frames referencing the lease_token and small result capsules. If a client reconnects before lease expiry it can present the lease_token to retrieve the last known result without re-invoking the tool.

4) Progressive structured output: support multiple fidelity lanes. Each output fragment carries a fidelity tag (draft | validated | committed). Clients can register an 'apply-as-you-go' policy (ui-friendly defaults) to render draft fragments while awaiting validation.

5) SDK ergonomics: thin client SDKs in JS/Python/Swift that expose:
   - connect(sessionConfig) -> Session object that emits: onFragment(fragment), onToolRequested(meta), onToolResult(result), onCheckpoint(token)
   - session.requestTool(toolId, params) -> Promise that resolves when server acknowledges the tool lease; returns lease token for later reconciliation
   - session.resume(hydrationToken) -> reconciles frames and reestablishes onFragment events
   - lightweight validators: isFragmentValid(fragment, schemaRef) -> boolean

Design details and examples:

Wire examples (high-level sketches):

- CONTROL: { type: "handshake", client_capabilities: ["compact", "resume"] }
- PAYLOAD: { type: "fragment", id: "f-23", lane: "draft", payload_type: "text", delta_to: "f-22", content: "..." }
- TOOL_CALL: { type: "tool_call", tool_id: "kb-search-v2", lease: "lt-99a", short_params: {q_hash: "abc123"} }
- TOOL_RESULT: { type: "tool_result", lease: "lt-99a", capsule_id: "tc-7", capsule_meta: {size_bytes: 128, schema: "kb-article-ref"} }

Edge and resume cases:

- Client disconnect after receiving a TOOL_CALL but before TOOL_RESULT: on reconnect, present the last checkpoint token. If lease still valid, server can re-emit TOOL_RESULT frame; if lease expired, server emits TOOL_EXPIRED and either a reference to cached result (if available) or a fallback action.

- Partial tool outputs: if a large tool result is produced incrementally, backends stream TOOL_RESULT partial capsules with sequence numbers and an is_final flag; fragments are reassembled by SDK automatically.

Telemetry and observability model:

Emit a small structured event set over the existing tracing pipeline:
- session.connect.duration_ms
- fragment.size_bytes
- tool.lease.latency_ms (time between TOOL_CALL and TOOL_RESULT first byte)
- tool.fallback.rate (percent of tool attempts that used fallback)
- resume.reconciliation.success (boolean)

These map to dashboards and an SLI that tracks end-to-end perceived latency and tool reliability. Each event includes minimal identifiers (model, route, session_type, region) and a hashed customer id for aggregation.

Backward-compatibility and migration:

- Server will support both legacy typed frames and the new compact surface; clients opt-in by advertising the "compact" capability during handshake. The server will continue to provide richer typed frames for internal heavy clients.

Operational playbook and fallbacks:

- If a reconciliation delta is > X KB (configurable), server will send a canonical checkpoint instead of many small deltas to avoid O(n) replay.
- Tool lease TTLs default to short values (e.g., 30s) for low-latency flows, but enterprise contracts may raise them (Dedicated/Private).

Security and privacy considerations:

- Hydration tokens are opaque and short-lived; do not contain PII.
- Tool result capsules that include customer data must obey route-level redaction policies; SDK provides hooks for client-side redaction validators.

Success metrics and KPIs:

- Integration time measured by number of engineering hours per integration (target: -50% at 3 months).
- Median client-visible time-to-first-fragment (target: < 150ms for 90th percentile on mobile profiles).
- Tool fallback rate (target: < 2% for default KB tools).
- Delta frame bytes per session (target: -30% vs current baseline).

Risks and open questions:

- Lease semantics complexity if tool backends live on a different lifetime model (sync vs async). Do we need a persisting store for certain enterprise tools?
- Schema drift for structured fragments: how do we version schemaRefs cheaply?
- Mobile SDK binary size impact if we include validators; consider moving validators to an optional plugin.

Rollout plan and next steps:

1) Prototype compact frames and hydration tokens in a staging runtime (2 sprints).
2) Build minimal JS/Swift client SDK that demonstrates resume and tool-lease retrieval (1 sprint).
3) Internal dogfood with 2 product teams (smart-reply, knowledge-assistant) and measure integration time and telemetry (4–6 weeks).
4) Iterate on lease defaults and checkpoint thresholds based on real-world delta sizes.

Open action items (owners):

- Draft protocol spec with byte-level frame examples (Ben Carlson)
- Implement SDK event surface and a small validation shim (Marta Gómez)
- Run a field pilot with Smart Reply (Daniel Wu)

Appendix: quick integration checklist for SDK users:

- Add dependency to hosted-compact-sdk (npm/pip/spm)
- Create sessionConfig: { route, model, desired_lanes: ["draft", "committed"] }
- Wire onFragment -> lightweightValidator -> UI render
- Listen for onToolRequested and call session.requestTool to reserve a lease
- Persist last checkpoint token periodically (every N fragments) and call session.resume(checkpoint) on reconnect

Notes to reviewers:

This is intentionally compact: the goal is a pragmatic, low-friction surface that can be shipped quickly and iterated on. Feedback: are the lease semantics simple enough? Are the fidelity lanes expressive but easy to reason about for a UI dev?

End of draft.
